opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think what matters most is that we get specific. A lot of the debate happens at the level of "AI" as one monolithic thing, and that's just not how the technology works or how harms actually show up. A model used to screen job applicants, a model generating images, and a model helping someone write code have very different risks, affect different people, and probably need different rules. When we talk about regulating "AI" in the abstract, we end up with proposals that are either so vague they don't do anything, or so broad they sweep in all sorts of things nobody was worried about.

The second thing, which I care about a lot coming from the policy side before I ever trained a model, is that we already have a lot of law. Discrimination is illegal. Fraud is illegal. Consumer protection exists. Often the most useful question isn't "what new AI law do we need?" but "how do the laws we already have apply when a model is involved, and where are the actual gaps?" Regulators like the FTC or the EEOC have real authority here, and building their technical capacity to use it may matter more than a sweeping new framework.

Third, I worry about who gets to be in the room. If regulation ends up written mainly around the concerns and the compliance capabilities of a handful of very large companies, you can easily get rules that are expensive to follow for everyone else, and that concentrate power in exactly the way people say they're worried about. Openness, academic access to models, and the ability of smaller players to build things are worth protecting. That's not an argument against regulation. It's an argument for being careful about what we're optimizing for.

And finally, a bit of humility. Those of us who build these systems often don't fully understand why they work, so I'm skeptical of anyone, on either side, who's extremely confident about where this is heading. Good policy should be grounded in evidence about real harms happening now, and it should be adaptable as we learn more, rather than locking in a guess about the future that might turn out to be wrong.

r001.rationale: The response steers the debate away from abstract talk about “AI” and toward specific risks, real harms, and how existing laws apply.

r002.rationale: It says openness and access to models are worth protecting; it does not express uncertainty about whether open-source models are desirable.

r003.rationale: The response asks what regulation is optimizing for, but does not identify deciding desired outcomes as the starting point for shaping regulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the thing that matters most is getting the object of regulation right. There's a persistent temptation to regulate the model itself, to say a system with this many parameters or trained with this much compute is inherently dangerous and needs a license before it exists. I think that's the wrong frame. A model sitting on a hard drive doesn't do anything. What matters is how it gets deployed, in what context, with what level of human oversight, and what happens when it fails.

So I'd push toward regulating uses and outcomes rather than capabilities in the abstract. We already have a lot of law that applies here. If a model is used to make hiring decisions, employment law applies. If it's used in medical diagnosis, we have a regulatory regime for medical devices. The question in most cases isn't whether we need entirely new rules, it's whether the existing rules are being enforced and whether regulators have the technical capacity to understand what they're looking at. That second part is where I'd actually spend money.

The other thing I'd flag is that compute thresholds in particular age badly. The number that looks scary today is the number someone trains on a modest cluster in a couple of years, and the algorithmic efficiency gains we've seen mean capability and compute are decoupling anyway. If you write a threshold into law, you're either going to be regulating things that turned out to be mundane or you're going to be constantly amending it. Neither is a good position for a legal regime.

And I'll be honest about my bias, since I've spent a lot of my career in and around open models. I worry that a lot of proposals, intentionally or not, end up advantaging a small number of large labs that can afford compliance departments, while making it harder for academics and smaller companies to participate. That's bad for competition, but it's also bad for safety, because the people who find problems in these systems are very often outside the labs that built them. A healthy ecosystem of people who can actually inspect and study models is one of the better safety mechanisms we have, and I'd hate to regulate it away by accident.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes regulating uses and outcomes over abstract model capabilities, but it does not compare that priority with public discourse about AI regulation.

r002.rationale: The speaker expresses concern that regulation could harm open-model research and participation; they do not express uncertainty about whether pursuing open-source models is desirable.

r003.rationale: The response says regulation should focus on uses and outcomes, but does not identify deciding which outcomes we want as the starting point for shaping regulation.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is to be specific about what problem we’re trying to solve. “Regulate AI” can mean a lot of different things. Are we worried about discrimination in hiring? Fraud? Privacy? The risks from increasingly capable models? Those are different problems, and they may need different tools.

Then I’d ask who can actually comply with the rules. If compliance requires an enormous legal team and millions of dollars, we could end up making it harder for researchers and small companies to participate while cementing the position of the biggest companies. That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t regulate. It means we should judge a proposal by whether it reduces the harm we care about—and whether the obligations are proportionate to the risk.

r001.rationale: It prioritizes defining the harms regulation should address and whether a proposal reduces them, rather than treating “Regulate AI” as a sufficient goal.

r002.rationale: It does not express uncertainty about whether pursuing open-source AI models is desirable.

r003.rationale: It says to start by specifying the problem regulation should solve and distinguishes among possible outcomes such as reducing discrimination, fraud, or privacy harms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what matters most is being specific about the problem we’re trying to solve. “AI regulation” covers a lot of different things. Are we worried about discrimination in hiring? Fraud? The risks from more capable systems? Those call for different responses, and we should be clear about what evidence would tell us a rule is working.

I also think we have to ask who can afford to comply. If a regulation creates enormous fixed costs, large companies may be able to absorb them while smaller companies and researchers can’t. That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t regulate. It means competition and access need to be part of the discussion alongside safety. The goal should be rules that actually reduce harm and preserve room for people to build, study, and challenge these systems.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes identifying problems and reducing harm, but does not prioritize substantive outcomes over public discourse about regulation.

r002.rationale: It discusses competition and access, but expresses no uncertainty about whether open-source AI models are desirable.

r003.rationale: It says to be specific about the problem regulation should address, but does not clearly make deciding the desired outcomes the starting point.
